text: And the citizen and Bloom having an argument about the point, the brothers Sheares and Wolfe Tone beyond on Arbour Hill and Robert Emmet and die for your country, the Tommy Moore touch about Sara Curran and she’s far from the land. And Bloom, of course, with his knockmedown cigar putting on swank with his lardy face. Phenomenon! The fat heap he married is a nice old phenomenon with a back on her like a ballalley. Time they were stopping up in the _City Arms_ pisser Burke told me there was an old one there with a cracked loodheramaun of a nephew and Bloom trying to get the soft side of her doing the mollycoddle playing bézique to come in for a bit of the wampum in her will and not eating meat of a Friday because the old one was always thumping her craw and taking the lout out for a walk. And one time he led him the rounds of Dublin and, by the holy farmer, he never cried crack till he brought him home as drunk as a boiled owl and he said he did it to teach him the evils of alcohol and by herrings, if the three women didn’t near roast him, it’s a queer story, the old one, Bloom’s wife and Mrs O’Dowd that kept the hotel. Jesus, I had to laugh at pisser Burke taking them off chewing the fat. And Bloom with his _but don’t you see?_ and _but on the other hand_. And sure, more be token, the lout I’m told was in Power’s after, the blender’s, round in Cope street going home footless in a cab five times in the week after drinking his way through all the samples in the bloody establishment. Phenomenon!
source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose is driven by active verbs and participles — putting, doing, playing, thumping, drinking, chewing, roast, led, brought — with human agents performing concrete actions. Nominalizations are rare; even abstract concepts like 'the evils of alcohol' arrive embedded in action sequences rather than as structural load-bearers.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage is strung together almost entirely by 'and,' accumulating incidents, names, and observations in coordinate chains without hierarchical subordination. Even the embedded narrative about the lout is delivered as a flat sequence of coordinated clauses rather than a structured subordinate argument.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive immediately and observations pile up afterward in trailing coordinate chains — 'And Bloom with his knockmedown cigar putting on swank,' 'And one time he led him the rounds of Dublin and...' There is no suspension of the main clause; the prose rushes forward without withholding.
claude_justifications.voice: This prose is saturated with a specific oral personality — the sneering Dublin gossip voice, with its italicized mimicry ('but don't you see?'), its exclamatory punctuation ('Phenomenon!'), its oaths ('by the holy farmer,' 'by herrings'), and its rhythmic contempt. Every sentence has a natural stress pattern and a performable sneer.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The diction is overwhelmingly demotic and Anglo-Irish vernacular — 'knockmedown,' 'lardy,' 'pisser,' 'loodheramaun,' 'wampum,' 'footless,' 'boiled owl.' Latinate vocabulary is almost entirely absent; the register is the spoken street-level idiom of early twentieth-century Dublin.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws constant attention to its own surface through slang coinages, italicized direct quotation, repeated exclamatory framing ('Phenomenon!'), rhythmic accumulation, and the sheer density of proper nouns and cultural references that foreground the narrator's voice as a constructed verbal performance rather than a transparent window onto events.

text: With this came up Lenehan to the feet of the table to say how the letter was in that night’s gazette and he made a show to find it about him (for he swore with an oath that he had been at pains about it) but on Stephen’s persuasion he gave over the search and was bidden to sit near by which he did mighty brisk. He was a kind of sport gentleman that went for a merryandrew or honest pickle and what belonged of women, horseflesh or hot scandal he had it pat. To tell the truth he was mean in fortunes and for the most part hankered about the coffeehouses and low taverns with crimps, ostlers, bookies, Paul’s men, runners, flatcaps, waistcoateers, ladies of the bagnio and other rogues of the game or with a chanceable catchpole or a tipstaff often at nights till broad day of whom he picked up between his sackpossets much loose gossip. He took his ordinary at a boilingcook’s and if he had but gotten into him a mess of broken victuals or a platter of tripes with a bare tester in his purse he could always bring himself off with his tongue, some randy quip he had from a punk or whatnot that every mother’s son of them would burst their sides. The other, Costello that is, hearing this talk asked was it poetry or a tale. Faith, no, he says, Frank (that was his name), ’tis all about Kerry cows that are to be butchered along of the plague. But they can go hang, says he with a wink, for me with their bully beef, a pox on it. There’s as good fish in this tin as ever came out of it and very friendly he offered to take of some salty sprats that stood by which he had eyed wishly in the meantime and found the place which was indeed the chief design of his embassy as he was sharpset. _Mort aux vaches_, says Frank then in the French language that had been indentured to a brandyshipper that has a winelodge in Bordeaux and he spoke French like a gentleman too.
source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose is driven by active verbs and human agents throughout — 'came up,' 'swore,' 'gave over,' 'hankered,' 'picked up,' 'brought himself off,' 'offered to take' — with characters doing things in rapid succession. Nominalizations are rare; even abstract qualities like 'fortunes' and 'design' appear embedded in action-forward clauses.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are strung together in long coordinate chains through 'and,' 'or,' and 'but,' with only light subordination via 'that' and 'which' relative clauses. The catalogue of 'crimps, ostlers, bookies, Paul's men, runners, flatcaps' and the serial 'and he... and he...' rhythm are quintessentially paratactic.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive immediately and qualifications trail behind in appositives, parenthetical asides, and coordinate additions — 'He was a kind of sport gentleman that went for a merryandrew or honest pickle and what belonged of women, horseflesh or hot scandal he had it pat.' Nothing is suspended; the prose accumulates forward.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is saturated with oral performance cues — direct speech, oaths ('he swore with an oath'), asides in parentheses, winks, quips, and the narrator's own interjections ('To tell the truth,' 'Faith, no'). It rewards and almost demands reading aloud, with natural rises, pauses, and comic emphases throughout.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The passage deliberately mixes registers: archaic mock-formal constructions ('he was bidden to sit,' 'his embassy,' 'sharpset') jostle against low tavern slang ('punk,' 'randy quip,' 'bully beef,' 'a pox on it') and cant vocabulary ('crimps,' 'flatcaps,' 'waistcoateers'). The mixing is itself the stylistic point — a burlesque of elevated prose applied to low life.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose constantly draws attention to its own surface through archaic diction, cant vocabulary, comic catalogues, embedded proverbs ('as good fish in this tin'), mock-heroic periphrasis ('the chief design of his embassy'), and the sudden French intrusion at the close. The language is a deliberate stylistic performance — a pastiche of seventeenth-century prose — that foregrounds itself as artifice.

text: The understanding may be a faculty for the production of unity of phenomena by virtue of rules; the reason is a faculty for the production of unity of rules (of the understanding) under principles. Reason, therefore, never applies directly to experience, or to any sensuous object; its object is, on the contrary, the understanding, to the manifold cognition of which it gives a unity à priori by means of conceptions—a unity which may be called rational unity, and which is of a nature very different from that of the unity produced by the understanding. The above is the general conception of the faculty of reason, in so far as it has been possible to make it comprehensible in the absence of examples. These will be given in the sequel.
source: John Henry Newman, The Idea of a University

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose is almost entirely driven by abstract nominalizations — understanding, production, unity, phenomena, reason, principles, cognition, conception — chained through prepositional phrases ('for the production of unity of phenomena by virtue of rules'). The few verbs present ('applies,' 'gives,' 'called') are weak copulas or near-copulas serving to link noun clusters rather than to drive action.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are embedded through 'which,' 'by means of,' 'in so far as,' and participial constructions, creating multiple levels of subordination. The second sentence in particular layers three relative clauses inside each other before resolving.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The passage mixes both tendencies: the opening definitional sentences deliver their main predications early and trail qualifications (running), while the long second sentence suspends resolution through embedded relative clauses and appositives before arriving at the final qualification about the nature of rational unity (periodic).
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is almost entirely resistant to vocal performance — there are no natural emphases, no dynamic range, no personality behind the statement. The flat, definitional evenness of 'the understanding is a faculty for the production of' makes any attempt at expressive reading feel absurd.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Exclusively Latinate and technical philosophical diction throughout: 'faculty,' 'phenomena,' 'sensuous,' 'cognition,' 'conceptions,' 'à priori,' 'rational unity.' No Anglo-Saxon plainness anywhere in the passage.
claude_justifications.opacity: Despite the extreme abstraction and syntactic density, the prose draws no attention to its own surface — there are no sound patterns, rhetorical figures, or self-conscious structural display. The language is purely instrumental, serving the conceptual argument without foregrounding itself as language.

text: This series of books will include in complete editions those masterpieces of English Literature that are best adapted for the use of schools and colleges. The editors of the several volumes will be chosen for their special qualifications in connection with the texts to be issued under their individual supervision, but familiarity with the practical needs of the classroom, no less than sound scholarship, will characterize the editing of every book in the series. In connection with each text, a critical and historical introduction, including a sketch of the life of the author and his relation to the thought of his time, critical opinions of the work in question chosen from the great body of English criticism, and, where possible, a portrait of the author, will be given. Ample explanatory notes of such passages in the text as call for special attention will be supplied, but irrelevant annotation and explanations of the obvious will be rigidly excluded.
source: John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose is dense with nominalizations and noun phrases: 'special qualifications,' 'individual supervision,' 'sound scholarship,' 'critical and historical introduction,' 'explanatory notes,' 'irrelevant annotation.' Verbs are largely weak copulas or passives ('will be chosen,' 'will be given,' 'will be supplied') that serve as mere connectors between noun clusters.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are embedded through 'that,' 'which,' 'including,' and participial constructions, creating layered subordination — particularly in the long third sentence, which nests multiple relative and participial phrases inside the main predication.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The third and fourth sentences are strongly periodic: long chains of qualifying material ('including a sketch... critical opinions... and, where possible, a portrait') accumulate before the main verb 'will be given' arrives. The reader must hold multiple suspended elements before the predication resolves.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is entirely impersonal — no first-person address, no rhetorical gesture toward a reader, no natural stress points or dynamic range. The passive constructions ('will be chosen,' 'will be excluded') flatten any performable energy into institutional announcement.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Formal Latinate diction throughout: 'qualifications,' 'supervision,' 'scholarship,' 'annotation,' 'characterize,' 'rigidly excluded.' The register is that of official editorial or publishing prospectus — ceremonious and impersonal.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws no attention to its own surface — no sound patterns, rhetorical figures, or structural display. The language is purely instrumental, serving to enumerate editorial policies without any self-conscious formal gesture.

text: These, then, are the three analogies of experience. They are nothing more than principles of the determination of the existence of phenomena in time, according to the three modi of this determination; to wit, the relation to time itself as a quantity (the quantity of existence, that is, duration), the relation in time as a series or succession, finally, the relation in time as the complex of all existence (simultaneity). This unity of determination in regard to time is thoroughly dynamical; that is to say, time is not considered as that in which experience determines immediately to every existence its position; for this is impossible, inasmuch as absolute time is not an object of perception, by means of which phenomena can be connected with each other. On the contrary, the rule of the understanding, through which alone the existence of phenomena can receive synthetical unity as regards relations of time, determines for every phenomenon its position in time, and consequently à priori, and with validity for all and every time.
source: John Henry Newman, The Idea of a University

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The passage is saturated with nominalizations and abstract nouns: determination, existence, phenomena, succession, simultaneity, perception, unity, validity. Verbs are almost entirely copular or weakly transitive ('are,' 'is considered,' 'can receive,' 'determines'), serving mainly to link noun-chains rather than drive action.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are deeply embedded through 'that,' 'which,' 'inasmuch as,' 'as regards,' and participial constructions, creating multiple ranked levels of subordination. The passage builds hierarchical qualification upon qualification rather than coordinating in parallel chains.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Some sentences open with front-loaded qualifications that suspend the main predication ('for this is impossible, inasmuch as...'), while others deliver their main clause early and trail elaborations afterward ('time is not considered as that in which...'). Neither pattern dominates consistently.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is almost entirely unperformable — abstract, impersonal, and without natural emphatic peaks or dynamic range. There is no speaker behind the statement, only a logical apparatus; attempting vocal performance would feel absurd.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Heavily Latinate and technical throughout: 'synthetical unity,' 'dynamical,' 'phenomena,' 'simultaneity,' 'à priori.' The diction is philosophical-technical, the highest and most specialized register.
claude_justifications.opacity: Despite its extreme difficulty, the prose makes no self-conscious display of its own surface — no sound patterns, rhetorical figures, or structural performance. The language is purely instrumental, attempting to point through itself to logical content, however opaque that content may be conceptually.

text: [Transcriber's Note: Sir William Blackstone's _Commentaries on the Laws of England_ was first published in 1765-1769. It contains a number of archaic spellings (including "goaler" for "gaoler" and "it's" for "its") that have been preserved as they appear in the original. All such spellings have been verified using the Oxford English Dictionary. Inconsistencies in spelling, punctuation, hyphenation, capitalization, and italicization have also been preserved. Obvious printer errors have been preserved and marked with a [Transcriber's Note]. Long s in the original has been modernized as modern s. The archaic convention of placing quotation marks at the beginning of each line of a quotation has also been modernized to quotation marks only at the beginning and end of the quotation.] _THE following sheets contain the substance of a course of lectures on the laws of England, which were read by the author in the university of OXFORD. His original plan took it's rise in the year 1753: and, notwithstanding the novelty of such an attempt in this age and country, and the prejudices usually conceived against any innovations in the established mode of education, he had the satisfaction to find (and he acknowleges it with a mixture of pride and gratitude) that his endeavours were encouraged and patronized by those, both in the university and out of it, whose good opinion and esteem he was principally desirous to obtain._
source: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (Vol 1)

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Heavy nominalization throughout: 'substance of a course of lectures,' 'novelty of such an attempt,' 'prejudices usually conceived against any innovations in the established mode of education,' 'a mixture of pride and gratitude.' The prose moves through prepositional phrase chains anchored to abstract nouns rather than through active verbs.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The long central sentence embeds clause within clause — 'notwithstanding the novelty... and the prejudices... he had the satisfaction to find (and he acknowledges it...) that his endeavours were encouraged... by those... whose good opinion...' — creating multiple ranked levels of subordination held in suspension.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The main predication ('he had the satisfaction to find... that his endeavours were encouraged') is delayed behind a long front-loaded participial and prepositional structure ('notwithstanding the novelty of such an attempt... and the prejudices usually conceived...'), requiring the reader to hold considerable subordinate material before the resolution arrives.
claude_justifications.voice: The third-person self-reference ('the author,' 'he') creates a formal ceremonial distance that partially suppresses vocal performance, yet the parenthetical aside '(and he acknowledges it with a mixture of pride and gratitude)' introduces a personal warmth that invites mild emphasis and dynamic variation.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Consistently formal Latinate diction throughout: 'patronized,' 'endeavours,' 'innovations,' 'prejudices,' 'principally desirous,' 'notwithstanding.' The register is that of eighteenth-century learned prose, ceremonial and elevated.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose is largely transparent in that it serves its prefatory argument without conspicuous sound patterning, yet the elaborate suspended periodic structure and the self-conscious parenthetical aside draw mild attention to the prose surface as a formal rhetorical performance rather than plain communication.

text: AN indefinite number of these hundreds make up a county or shire. Shire is a Saxon word signifying a division; but a county, _comitatus_, is plainly derived from _comes_, the count of the Franks; that is, the earl, or alderman (as the Saxons called him) of the shire, to whom the government of it was intrusted. This he usually exercised by his deputy, still called in Latin _vice-comes_, and in English the sheriff, shrieve, or shire-reeve, signifying the officer of the shire; upon whom by process of time the civil administration of it is now totally devolved. In some counties there is an intermediate division, between the shire and the hundreds, as lathes in Kent, and rapes in Sussex, each of them containing about three or four hundreds apiece. These had formerly their lathe-reeves and rape-reeves, acting in subordination to the shire-reeve. Where a county is divided into _three_ of these intermediate jurisdictions, they are called trithings[e], which were antiently governed by a trithing-reeve. These trithings still subsist in the large county of York, where by an easy corruption they are denominated ridings; the north, the east, and the west-riding. The number of counties in England and Wales have been different at different times: at present there are forty in England, and twelve in Wales.
source: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (Vol 1)

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose is organized around nominal definitions and etymological derivations — 'division,' 'administration,' 'government,' 'corruption,' 'jurisdictions' — with verbs largely serving as copulas or passive constructions ('is derived,' 'is intrusted,' 'is now totally devolved'). The subject matter itself drives nominalization: this is a taxonomy of administrative units, and the prose enacts that taxonomy through noun-heavy structure.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage alternates between hypotactic relative clauses ('to whom the government of it was intrusted,' 'still called in Latin vice-comes') and paratactic enumeration ('the north, the east, and the west-riding'). Individual sentences tend toward hypotaxis, but the paragraph as a whole proceeds by coordinate accumulation of parallel facts.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Most sentences deliver their main predication early and then trail qualifications, etymological glosses, and parenthetical elaborations afterward — 'This he usually exercised by his deputy, still called in Latin vice-comes, and in English the sheriff...' The information accumulates after the main clause rather than suspending it.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose has a measured, lecturing quality that rewards careful oral delivery — the etymological asides and parenthetical glosses create natural pauses and mild emphasis — but the impersonal, definitional mode suppresses dramatic range and personal presence, keeping it short of strongly voiced.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Formal Latinate diction dominates: 'comitatus,' 'vice-comes,' 'intermediate jurisdictions,' 'civil administration,' 'subordination,' 'antiently.' The Latin etymologies are displayed rather than translated away, signaling a learned, legal-encyclopedic register throughout.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose is largely transparent in its expository function — it aims to convey information about administrative divisions — but the foregrounded etymological display (Saxon, Latin, and Norman derivations set in italics and explained) draws intermittent attention to language itself as an object of inquiry, creating moments of deliberate surface visibility.

text: IT there passes through the same forms as in the other house, (except engrossing, which is already done) and, if rejected, no more notice is taken, but it passes _sub silentio_, to prevent unbecoming altercations. But if it is agreed to, the lords send a message by two masters in chancery (or sometimes two of the judges) that they have agreed to the same: and the bill remains with the lords, if they have made no amendment to it. But if any amendments are made, such amendments are sent down with the bill to receive the concurrence of the commons. If the commons disagree to the amendments, a conference usually follows between members deputed from each house; who for the most part settle and adjust the difference: but, if both houses remain inflexible, the bill is dropped. If the commons agree to the amendments, the bill is sent back to the lords by one of the members, with a message to acquaint them therewith. The same forms are observed, _mutatis mutandis_, when the bill begins in the house of lords. And when both houses have done with the bill, it always is deposited in the house of peers, to wait the royal assent.
source: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (Vol 1)

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs drive the procedural logic throughout — passes, rejected, agreed, send, remains, settle, adjust, dropped, deposited — with human and institutional agents performing discrete actions. Nominalizations are present (concurrence, amendments, altercations) but subordinate to the verb-driven procedural chain.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage alternates between conditional hypotaxis ('if rejected... but if it is agreed... if the commons disagree') and paratactic coordination ('and the bill remains... and when both houses have done'). The conditional 'if/but if' structure creates a branching decision-tree logic that is neither purely embedded nor purely coordinate.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Most sentences deliver their main predication early and append qualifications afterward — 'the lords send a message by two masters in chancery (or sometimes two of the judges) that they have agreed.' The conditional 'if' clauses that open some sentences create mild periodicity, but the main clause typically arrives quickly.
claude_justifications.voice: The procedural enumeration and parallel 'if/but if' structure creates a readable, almost pedagogical rhythm that could be performed as a clear oral recitation, though without dramatic range or personal emphasis. The Latin insertions and parenthetical qualifications flatten the vocal texture somewhat.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Formal legal-parliamentary diction throughout: 'sub silentio,' 'mutatis mutandis,' 'engrossing,' 'masters in chancery,' 'royal assent,' 'concurrence.' The register is consistently elevated and technical, characteristic of eighteenth-century legal exposition.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose is entirely instrumental — it exists to convey procedural information and draws no attention to its own surface. The parallel conditional structure is functional rather than ornamental, and there are no sound patterns, rhetorical figures, or self-conscious stylistic display.

text: THE power and jurisdiction of parliament, says sir Edward Coke[c], is so transcendent and absolute, that it cannot be confined, either for causes or persons, within any bounds. And of this high court he adds, it may be truly said "_si antiquitatem spectes, est vetustissima; si dignitatem, est honoratissima; si juridictionem, est capacissima_." It hath sovereign and uncontrolable authority in making, confirming, enlarging, restraining, abrogating, repealing, reviving, and expounding of laws, concerning matters of all possible denominations, ecclesiastical, or temporal, civil, military, maritime, or criminal: this being the place where that absolute despotic power, which must in all governments reside somewhere, is entrusted by the constitution of these kingdoms. All mischiefs and grievances, operations and remedies, that transcend the ordinary course of the laws, are within the reach of this extraordinary tribunal. It can regulate or new model the succession to the crown; as was done in the reign of Henry VIII and William III. It can alter the established religion of the land; as was done in a variety of instances, in the reigns of king Henry VIII and his three children. It can change and create afresh even the constitution of the kingdom and of parliaments themselves; as was done by the act of union, and the several statutes for triennial and septennial elections. It can, in short, do every thing that is not naturally impossible; and therefore some have not scrupled to call it's power, by a figure rather too bold, the omnipotence of parliament. True it is, that what they do, no authority upon earth can undo. So that it is a matter most essential to the liberties of this kingdom, that such members be delegated to this important trust, as are most eminent for their probity, their fortitude, and their knowlege; for it was a known apothegm of the great lord treasurer Burleigh, "that England could never be ruined but by a parliament:" and, as sir Matthew Hale observes[d], this being the highest and greatest court, over which none other can have jurisdiction in the kingdom, if by any means a misgovernment should any way fall upon it, the subjects of this kingdom are left without all manner of remedy.
source: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (Vol 1)

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The passage contains significant nominalization ('jurisdiction,' 'denomination,' 'misgovernment,' 'omnipotence') and prepositional chains, but is also driven by strong active verbs in the anaphoric 'It can' series — 'regulate,' 'alter,' 'change,' 'create.' The two tendencies coexist rather than one dominating.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The 'It can... It can... It can...' series is strongly paratactic, coordinating parallel assertions in a rhetorical chain; but the surrounding sentences are hypotactic, embedding subordinate clauses through 'which,' 'that,' 'as,' and 'if,' creating multiple levels of qualification.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The 'It can' sentences are running — main predications arrive immediately and trail examples afterward. But the final long sentence is periodic, suspending its conclusion ('the subjects of this kingdom are left without all manner of remedy') behind a chain of conditional and participial qualifications.
claude_justifications.voice: The anaphoric 'It can... It can... It can...' series is built for oral delivery and rhetorical crescendo, with natural stress points and dynamic range. The embedded Latin quotation, the named authorities (Coke, Burleigh, Hale), and the closing apothegm all invite vocal performance and emphasis.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Formal Latinate diction throughout — 'transcendent,' 'jurisdiction,' 'ecclesiastical,' 'denominations,' 'abrogating,' 'despotic,' 'probity,' 'apothegm' — with embedded Latin and ceremonial legal register consistent with eighteenth-century parliamentary discourse.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws deliberate attention to its own surface through the anaphoric 'It can' series, the embedded Latin quotation with its triple superlative structure, the catalogue of gerunds ('making, confirming, enlarging, restraining, abrogating, repealing, reviving'), and the rhetorical figure of 'omnipotence of parliament' — all of which foreground structural and rhetorical display.

text: BUT the common law of England, being not committed to writing, but only handed down by tradition, use, and experience, was not so heartily relished by the foreign clergy; who came over hither in shoals during the reign of the conqueror and his two sons, and were utter strangers to our constitution as well as our language. And an accident, which soon after happened, had nearly completed it's ruin. A copy of Justinian's pandects, being newly[u] discovered at Amalfi, soon brought the civil law into vogue all over the west of Europe, where before it was quite laid aside[w] and in a manner forgotten; though some traces of it's authority remained in Italy[x] and the eastern provinces of the empire[y]. This now became in a particular manner the favourite of the popish clergy, who borrowed the method and many of the maxims of their canon law from this original. The study of it was introduced into several universities abroad, particularly that of Bologna; where exercises were performed, lectures read, and degrees conferred in this faculty, as in other branches of science: and many nations on the continent, just then beginning to recover from the convulsions consequent upon the overthrow of the Roman empire, and settling by degrees into peaceable forms of government, adopted the civil law, (being the best written system then extant) as the basis of their several constitutions; blending and interweaving it among their own feodal customs, in some places with a more extensive, in others a more confined authority[z].
source: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (Vol 1)

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Heavy nominalization throughout — tradition, experience, constitution, authority, convulsions, overthrow — chained with prepositional phrases ('of the empire,' 'of the conqueror,' 'of their canon law from this original'). Active verbs appear but are often passive or weak copulas ('was introduced,' 'were performed,' 'were conferred'), and the nominal weight dominates the prose's center of gravity.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses embed deeply through 'who,' 'which,' 'where,' 'being,' and participial constructions, creating multiple ranked levels of subordination within single sentences. The long final sentence is a showcase of hypotactic layering — nations adopting law, blending customs, qualified by parenthetical and participial phrases stacked inside each other.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The passage mixes both tendencies: some sentences open with front-loaded subordinate material ('A copy of Justinian's pandects, being newly discovered at Amalfi, soon brought...') that is mildly periodic, while others trail qualifications after an early main predication in running fashion. The final long sentence is strongly periodic, suspending its main verb 'adopted' behind a long participial buildup.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose carries a discernible authorial personality — the dry irony of 'not so heartily relished' and 'shoals' gives it some performable edge — but the long embedded clauses and passive constructions flatten the dynamic range, making sustained oral performance difficult without losing the thread.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Formal Latinate diction throughout: 'pandects,' 'faculty,' 'feodal,' 'constitutions,' 'convulsions consequent upon,' 'extensive authority.' The register is consistently elevated legal-historical prose, with no concession to plain Anglo-Saxon vocabulary.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose is largely transparent in that it serves its historical argument without conspicuous rhetorical display, but moments of deliberate stylistic choice surface — the sardonic 'in shoals,' the rhythmic tricolon 'exercises were performed, lectures read, and degrees conferred,' and the balanced antithesis of 'more extensive, in others a more confined authority' draw brief attention to the surface.

text: I didn’t hurry; I couldn’t if I’d a wanted to. I took one slow step at a time and there warn’t a sound, only I thought I could hear my heart. The dogs were as still as the humans, but they followed a little behind me. When I got to the three log doorsteps I heard them unlocking and unbarring and unbolting. I put my hand on the door and pushed it a little and a little more till somebody said, “There, that’s enough—put your head in.” I done it, but I judged they would take it off. The candle was on the floor, and there they all was, looking at me, and me at them, for about a quarter of a minute: Three big men with guns pointed at me, which made me wince, I tell you; the oldest, gray and about sixty, the other two thirty or more—all of them fine and handsome—and the sweetest old gray-headed lady, and back of her two young women which I couldn’t see right well. The old gentleman says:
source: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The passage is driven almost entirely by physical action verbs — hurry, took, thought, heard, unlocking, unbarring, unbolting, pushed, said, done, judged, wince, looking. Nouns are concrete and simple (door, candle, floor, guns), never nominalized or chained with prepositions.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are strung together with 'and' and 'but' in coordinate chains — 'and pushed it a little and a little more,' 'and there they all was, looking at me, and me at them.' The few subordinate clauses ('till somebody said,' 'which I couldn't see right well') are shallow and do not create embedded hierarchies.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive immediately and observations trail behind in coordinate chains — 'I took one slow step at a time and there warn't a sound,' 'The candle was on the floor, and there they all was.' Nothing is suspended or front-loaded with qualifying material.
claude_justifications.voice: The first-person vernacular voice is unmistakable and highly performable — 'which made me wince, I tell you' is a direct address to the listener, and the rhythms of 'unlocking and unbarring and unbolting' demand oral delivery with natural stress and pacing. The dialect itself is a performance register.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Consistently Anglo-Saxon and vernacular throughout — 'warn't,' 'I done it,' 'I judged,' 'gray-headed,' 'back of her.' No Latinate vocabulary; the diction is deliberately colloquial and regional.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws attention to its own surface through the triple polysyndeton of 'unlocking and unbarring and unbolting,' the rhythmic repetition of 'a little and a little more,' and the conspicuous dialect spelling — these are deliberate formal choices that foreground the language itself as a stylistic object.

text: It might correct the moral feelings of a numerous class of readers, to suppose a Review set on foot, the object of which should be to criticise all the chief works presented to the public by our ribbon-weavers, calico-printers, cabinet-makers, and china-manufacturers; which should be conducted in the same spirit, and take the same freedom with personal character, as our literary journals. They would scarcely, I think, deny their belief, not only that the genus irritabile would be found to include many other species besides that of bards; but that the irritability of trade would soon reduce the resentments of poets into mere shadow-fights in the comparison. Or is wealth the only rational object of human interest? Or even if this were admitted, has the poet no property in his works? Or is it a rare, or culpable case, that he who serves at the altar of the Muses, should be compelled to derive his maintenance from the altar, when too he has perhaps deliberately abandoned the fairest prospects of rank and opulence in order to devote himself, an entire and undistracted man, to the instruction or refinement of his fellow-citizens? Or, should we pass by all higher objects and motives, all disinterested benevolence, and even that ambition of lasting praise which is at once the crutch and ornament, which at once supports and betrays, the infirmity of human virtue,--is the character and property of the man, who labours for our intellectual pleasures, less entitled to a share of our fellow feeling, than that of the wine-merchant or milliner? Sensibility indeed, both quick and deep, is not only a characteristic feature, but may be deemed a component part, of genius. But it is not less an essential mark of true genius, that its sensibility is excited by any other cause more powerfully than by its own personal interests; for this plain reason, that the man of genius lives most in the ideal world, in which the present is still constituted by the future or the past; and because his feelings have been habitually associated with thoughts and images, to the number, clearness, and vivacity of which the sensation of self is always in an inverse proportion.
source: Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Biographia Literaria

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Abstract nominalizations proliferate throughout — irritability, resentments, maintenance, refinement, benevolence, sensibility, vivacity — often chained with prepositional phrases ('the instruction or refinement of his fellow-citizens,' 'the number, clearness, and vivacity of which'). Verbs are present but frequently serve as copulas or light connectives rather than driving action.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage is densely embedded through 'that,' 'which,' 'when,' 'in which,' 'because,' and participial constructions, creating multiple subordinate levels within single sentences. The long final sentence alone contains at least four nested subordinate clauses.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications are repeatedly delayed behind accumulating conditionals, qualifications, and subordinate material — most strikingly in the long rhetorical question beginning 'Or, should we pass by all higher objects' which suspends its resolution through a cascade of appositives and relative clauses before arriving at the main comparison. The serial 'Or is... Or even if... Or is it...' structure front-loads conditions throughout.
claude_justifications.voice: The repeated anaphoric 'Or' questions, the parenthetical asides, the rhetorical climaxes, and the deliberate antitheses ('at once the crutch and ornament, which at once supports and betrays') all demand vocal performance with natural emphases, pauses, and rising indignation. This is oratorical prose written to be felt as well as read.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Consistently Latinate and formal throughout: 'genus irritabile,' 'opulence,' 'disinterested benevolence,' 'undistracted,' 'vivacity,' 'inverse proportion.' The diction is elevated and ceremonial, with no concession to plain Anglo-Saxon vocabulary.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose foregrounds its own rhetorical surface through deliberate structural display: the anaphoric 'Or' series, the chiastic antithesis ('supports and betrays'), the Latin tag, the self-conscious parallelism of 'quick and deep,' 'number, clearness, and vivacity.' The writing calls attention to itself as performance rather than letting the reader look through to content alone.

text: Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation, when beholding the white depths of the milky way? Or is it, that as in essence whiteness is not so much a colour as the visible absence of colour; and at the same time the concrete of all colours; is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows—a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink? And when we consider that other theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly hues—every stately or lovely emblazoning—the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods; yea, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls; all these are but subtile deceits, not actually inherent in substances, but only laid on from without; so that all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within; and when we proceed further, and consider that the mystical cosmetic which produces every one of her hues, the great principle of light, for ever remains white or colorless in itself, and if operating without medium upon matter, would touch all objects, even tulips and roses, with its own blank tinge—pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper; and like wilful travellers in Lapland, who refuse to wear coloured and colouring glasses upon their eyes, so the wretched infidel gazes himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps all the prospect around him. And of all these things the Albino whale was the symbol. Wonder ye then at the fiery hunt?
source: Herman Melville, Moby-Dick

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The passage contains significant nominalization ('indefiniteness,' 'annihilation,' 'emblazoning,' 'allurements') but is equally driven by active and participial verbs — 'stabs,' 'shrink,' 'paints,' 'wraps,' 'gazes,' 'pondering' — that carry genuine rhetorical force. Neither mode dominates; the nouns accumulate weight while the verbs deliver the blows.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The long central sentence is a massive hypotactic construction — 'when we consider... that all other earthly hues... all these are but subtile deceits... and when we proceed further... pondering all this' — stacking subordinate clauses, relative clauses, and participial phrases inside each other across many lines before resolving. Even the shorter sentences use embedded 'that' and 'which' constructions.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The dominant structural gesture is massive suspension: the great central sentence withholds its main predication ('the palsied universe lies before us a leper') behind an enormous accumulation of 'when... and when... pondering all this' — a classic periodic architecture that forces the reader to hold the entire weight of the argument before the resolution arrives.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is intensely performable — rhetorical questions open and close, direct address ('Wonder ye then'), exclamatory compression ('a leper'), and the rhythmic catalogues ('sunset skies and woods; yea, and the gilded velvets of butterflies') all demand vocal emphasis, dynamic range, and a preacher's cadence. The 'yea' alone signals oral performance.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The passage moves between high Latinate diction ('indefiniteness,' 'immensities,' 'cosmetic,' 'mystical,' 'inherent') and sudden plain Anglo-Saxon concretions ('stabs,' 'blank,' 'shroud,' 'leper,' 'blind') — the collision between registers is itself a rhetorical strategy, the sublime crashing into the visceral.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose constantly draws attention to its own surface: the anaphoric 'Or is it... is it for these reasons'; the chiasmic 'colourless, all-colour'; the extended simile of the harlot and charnel-house; the alliterative 'palsied... prospect'; the closing rhetorical question as formal seal. This is prose that performs its own rhetoric visibly and deliberately.
