text: It could never be more truly said than of the first remedy, that it was worse than the disease. Liberty is to faction what air is to fire, an aliment without which it instantly expires. But it could not be less folly to abolish liberty, which is essential to political life, because it nourishes faction, than it would be to wish the annihilation of air, which is essential to animal life, because it imparts to fire its destructive agency. The second expedient is as impracticable as the first would be unwise. As long as the reason of man continues fallible, and he is at liberty to exercise it, different opinions will be formed. As long as the connection subsists between his reason and his self-love, his opinions and his passions will have a reciprocal influence on each other; and the former will be objects to which the latter will attach themselves. The diversity in the faculties of men, from which the rights of property originate, is not less an insuperable obstacle to a uniformity of interests. The protection of these faculties is the first object of government. From the protection of different and unequal faculties of acquiring property, the possession of different degrees and kinds of property immediately results; and from the influence of these on the sentiments and views of the respective proprietors, ensues a division of the society into different interests and parties.
source: Alexander Hamilton et al., The Federalist Papers

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose is dense with nominalizations and abstract nouns — liberty, faction, annihilation, diversity, uniformity, protection, possession, division — chained through prepositional phrases ('from the protection of different and unequal faculties of acquiring property'). Verbs are largely copular or weak ('is,' 'results,' 'ensues'), with the nouns carrying the argumentative weight.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are systematically embedded through 'which,' 'because,' 'as long as,' 'from which,' and 'and from' constructions, creating ranked hierarchical subordination. The analogical structure ('Liberty is to faction what air is to fire') itself requires nested relational embedding.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The passage alternates strategies: some sentences are periodic, suspending the main predication behind conditional or comparative front-loading ('As long as... different opinions will be formed'), while others are running, delivering the main clause early and trailing elaboration ('Liberty is to faction what air is to fire, an aliment without which it instantly expires').
claude_justifications.voice: The prose carries strong rhetorical performance — the analogy ('Liberty is to faction what air is to fire') invites emphatic delivery, and the parallel 'As long as' constructions create a rising cadence that rewards oral stress. The antithetical structures ('worse than the disease,' 'less folly... than it would be') provide natural dynamic contrast.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Formal Latinate diction throughout: 'aliment,' 'expedient,' 'impracticable,' 'annihilation,' 'insuperable,' 'reciprocal,' 'proprietors.' The register is consistently elevated, befitting deliberative political argument.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws sustained attention to its own surface through the extended analogy (liberty:faction::air:fire), the parallel 'As long as' anaphora, and the antithetical chiasmic structures. These rhetorical figures are conspicuous formal displays, not merely instrumental vehicles for content.

text: A stranger to our politics, who was to read our newspapers at the present juncture, without having previously inspected the plan reported by the convention, would be naturally led to one of two conclusions: either that it contained a positive injunction, that standing armies should be kept up in time of peace; or that it vested in the EXECUTIVE the whole power of levying troops, without subjecting his discretion, in any shape, to the control of the legislature. If he came afterwards to peruse the plan itself, he would be surprised to discover, that neither the one nor the other was the case; that the whole power of raising armies was lodged in the LEGISLATURE, not in the EXECUTIVE; that this legislature was to be a popular body, consisting of the representatives of the people periodically elected; and that instead of the provision he had supposed in favor of standing armies, there was to be found, in respect to this object, an important qualification even of the legislative discretion, in that clause which forbids the appropriation of money for the support of an army for any longer period than two years a precaution which, upon a nearer view of it, will appear to be a great and real security against the keeping up of troops without evident necessity.
source: Alexander Hamilton et al., The Federalist Papers

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Heavy nominalization throughout — 'injunction,' 'discretion,' 'control,' 'provision,' 'qualification,' 'appropriation,' 'precaution,' 'security' — chained with prepositional phrases ('in favor of,' 'in respect to,' 'for the support of'). Verbs are largely copular or passive ('was lodged,' 'was to be found'), suppressing agency in favor of nominal constructions.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage is built on deep subordination — 'who was to read,' 'without having previously inspected,' 'that it contained,' 'that neither the one nor the other,' 'that this legislature was,' 'that instead of,' 'which forbids,' 'which upon a nearer view' — creating multiple nested levels of embedded clauses that require the reader to track several simultaneous syntactic threads.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The opening sentence is a textbook periodic construction: the subject ('A stranger') is immediately buried under a long conditional apparatus ('who was to read... without having previously inspected... would be naturally led') before the main predication resolves. The second sentence similarly front-loads the conditional ('If he came afterwards to peruse') before delivering its payload of discoveries in a long trailing series.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose carries a forensic, argumentative personality — the rhetorical setup of the imagined 'stranger,' the emphatic capitalization of LEGISLATURE and EXECUTIVE, and the cumulative 'that... that... that' anaphora give it performable rhythm and a sense of controlled indignation. However, the density of subordination and nominalization flattens the dynamic range, preventing full vocal expressiveness.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Formal Latinate diction throughout: 'injunction,' 'discretion,' 'legislature,' 'periodically,' 'appropriation,' 'precaution,' 'qualification.' The register is consistently elevated, befitting constitutional argument addressed to an educated public readership.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose is largely transparent in that it serves its argumentative purpose without calling attention to its own surface, but the anaphoric 'that... that... that' series and the emphatic capitalization of LEGISLATURE/EXECUTIVE are deliberate rhetorical figures that briefly foreground the language itself as a structural and persuasive device.

text: This sentence of death, which, they tell us, was thus passed upon Adam, must either have meant dying naturally, that is, ceasing to live, or have meant what these mythologists call damnation; and consequently, the act of dying on the part of Jesus Christ, must, according to their system, apply as a prevention to one or other of these two things happening to Adam and to us. That it does not prevent our dying is evident, because we all die; and if their accounts of longevity be true, men die faster since the crucifixion than before: and with respect to the second explanation, (including with it the natural death of Jesus Christ as a substitute for the eternal death or damnation of all mankind,) it is impertinently representing the Creator as coming off, or revoking the sentence, by a pun or a quibble upon the word death. That manufacturer of, quibbles, St. Paul, if he wrote the books that bear his name, has helped this quibble on by making another quibble upon the word Adam. He makes there to be two Adams; the one who sins in fact, and suffers by proxy; the other who sins by proxy, and suffers in fact. A religion thus interlarded with quibble, subterfuge, and pun, has a tendency to instruct its professors in the practice of these arts. They acquire the habit without being aware of the cause.
source: Thomas Paine, Rights of Man

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs carry real argumentative force — 'does not prevent,' 'die faster,' 'makes there to be,' 'acquire the habit' — but nominalizations and abstract nouns also appear throughout: 'prevention,' 'longevity,' 'crucifixion,' 'damnation,' 'explanation.' Neither mode dominates; the prose alternates between conceptual noun-clusters and punchy verbal assertions.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The long opening sentence is deeply hypotactic, with nested conditionals, parenthetical elaborations, and 'which/that/because' subordination stacked several levels deep. But the later sentences — 'That it does not prevent our dying is evident, because we all die' and 'They acquire the habit without being aware of the cause' — are comparatively flat and coordinate, creating a rhythm that alternates between embedded complexity and blunt simplicity.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The opening sentence is strongly periodic, suspending its main predication behind a long conditional apparatus ('must either have meant... or have meant... and consequently... must... apply'). Later sentences flip to running structure, delivering their main claim immediately and trailing qualifications: 'That it does not prevent our dying is evident, because we all die.'
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is saturated with performable contempt — 'these mythologists,' 'That manufacturer of quibbles, St. Paul,' 'a pun or a quibble upon the word death.' There are natural stress points, rhetorical pauses, and a speaker's personality behind every clause; the sarcasm demands vocal delivery.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Latinate theological vocabulary ('damnation,' 'longevity,' 'crucifixion,' 'impertinently,' 'subterfuge') coexists with deliberately colloquial, deflating Anglo-Saxon terms ('pun,' 'quibble,' 'coming off,' 'helped this quibble on'). The mixing is strategic — the low diction is deployed to mock the high.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws conspicuous attention to its own rhetorical surface through the obsessive repetition of 'quibble' (five times), the chiastic formulation 'sins in fact / suffers by proxy; sins by proxy / suffers in fact,' and the theatrical naming of St. Paul as 'that manufacturer of quibbles.' These are deliberate structural and sonic displays, not transparent vehicles for argument.

text: Quitting these reflections, I proceed to other matters. After I had made myself master of the use of the globes, and of the orrery, [NOTE by Paine: As this book may fall into the bands of persons who do not know what an orrery is, it is for their information I add this note, as the name gives no idea of the uses of the thing. The orrery has its name from the person who invented it. It is a machinery of clock-work, representing the universe in miniature: and in which the revolution of the earth round itself and round the sun, the revolution of the moon round the earth, the revolution of the planets round the sun, their relative distances from the sun, as the center of the whole system, their relative distances from each other, and their different magnitudes, are represented as they really exist in what we call the heavens.—Author.] and conceived an idea of the infinity of space, and of the eternal divisibility of matter, and obtained, at least, a general knowledge of what was called natural philosophy, I began to compare, or, as I have before said, to confront, the internal evidence those things afford with the christian system of faith.
source: Thomas Paine, Rights of Man

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The passage is heavily nominalized — 'the revolution of the earth,' 'the eternal divisibility of matter,' 'the infinity of space,' 'a general knowledge of what was called natural philosophy' — with long prepositional chains accumulating around abstract nouns. The main verbs ('had made,' 'conceived,' 'obtained,' 'began to compare') are sparse anchors in a sea of noun phrases.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The main sentence is a single enormous hypotactic structure in which multiple subordinate 'after' and 'and' clauses are embedded before the main predication arrives; the parenthetical note itself is densely hypotactic, with 'in which' introducing a long relative clause that accumulates parallel noun phrases through repeated 'the revolution of' constructions.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The outer sentence withholds its main clause ('I began to compare... the internal evidence... with the christian system of faith') until after an enormous accumulation of subordinate material — 'After I had made myself master of... and conceived... and obtained' — forcing the reader to hold multiple suspended elements before resolution arrives.
claude_justifications.voice: The first-person address ('I proceed,' 'I began to compare') and the direct authorial intrusion of the footnote ('it is for their information I add this note') give the prose a personal, performable quality, but the long enumerative lists within the parenthetical flatten into a recitative drone that resists dynamic vocal range.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The diction is neither ceremonially Latinate nor plainly Anglo-Saxon — terms like 'divisibility,' 'revolution,' and 'magnitudes' sit alongside plain constructions like 'round itself' and 'as they really exist,' producing a practical, instructional middle register characteristic of Enlightenment popular science writing.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose is largely transparent in its aim — it wants to convey information and logical sequence — but the deliberate structural display of the parenthetical note (with its anaphoric repetition of 'the revolution of... the revolution of... the revolution of') draws attention to the surface as a rhetorical enumeration, and the meta-linguistic gesture of the footnote itself foregrounds the author's presence as a self-conscious stylist.

text: “Well, well, well,--now who would ever have thought it? One whole duke and six dukelets; why, Sandy, it was an elegant haul. Knight-errantry is a most chuckle-headed trade, and it is tedious hard work, too, but I begin to see that there _is_ money in it, after all, if you have luck. Not that I would ever engage in it as a business, for I wouldn't. No sound and legitimate business can be established on a basis of speculation. A successful whirl in the knight-errantry line--now what is it when you blow away the nonsense and come down to the cold facts? It's just a corner in pork, that's all, and you can't make anything else out of it. You're rich--yes,--suddenly rich--for about a day, maybe a week; then somebody corners the market on _you_, and down goes your bucket-shop; ain't that so, Sandy?”
source: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs and verbal idioms drive the passage — 'blow away,' 'come down,' 'corners the market,' 'goes your bucket-shop' — with minimal nominalization. Even abstract concepts are rendered through action: 'you can't make anything else out of it.'
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are strung together with 'and,' 'but,' 'then,' and dashes in loose coordinate chains rather than embedded subordination. The syntax mimics spoken improvisation, moving forward by addition rather than hierarchical embedding.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive immediately and qualifications trail behind — 'You're rich--yes,--suddenly rich--for about a day, maybe a week; then somebody corners the market on you.' No suspended main clauses; the prose rushes forward and corrects itself as it goes.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is saturated with performable personality — the triple 'Well, well, well,' the italicized stress on 'is' and 'you,' the rhetorical question closing the passage. A reader can hear the speaker's rising and falling enthusiasm, his mock-businesslike deflation, his conspiratorial address to Sandy.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Predominantly Anglo-Saxon and vernacular diction: 'chuckle-headed,' 'haul,' 'bucket-shop,' 'pork,' 'blow away.' The one Latinate gesture ('speculation,' 'legitimate') is deployed ironically to mock the pretension of formal business language.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws constant attention to its own surface through rhetorical figures — the triple opening, the italics, the extended market metaphor applied to knight-errantry, the tag question. The structural display of vernacular performance is itself the point, not merely a vehicle for content.

text: They had abundance of tripes, as you have heard, and they were so delicious, that everyone licked his fingers. But the mischief was this, that, for all men could do, there was no possibility to keep them long in that relish; for in a very short while they would have stunk, which had been an undecent thing. It was therefore concluded, that they should be all of them gulched up, without losing anything. To this effect they invited all the burghers of Sainais, of Suille, of the Roche-Clermaud, of Vaugaudry, without omitting the Coudray, Monpensier, the Gue de Vede, and other their neighbours, all stiff drinkers, brave fellows, and good players at the kyles. The good man Grangousier took great pleasure in their company, and commanded there should be no want nor pinching for anything. Nevertheless he bade his wife eat sparingly, because she was near her time, and that these tripes were no very commendable meat. They would fain, said he, be at the chewing of ordure, that would eat the case wherein it was. Notwithstanding these admonitions, she did eat sixteen quarters, two bushels, three pecks and a pipkin full. O the fair fecality wherewith she swelled, by the ingrediency of such shitten stuff!
source: Thomas De Quincey, Confessions of an English Opium-Eater

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs drive the passage — licked, stunk, concluded, invited, took, commanded, bade, eat, swelled — with human agents performing concrete actions. Nominalizations appear occasionally ('ingrediency,' 'fecality') but as comic flourishes rather than structural load-bearers.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage alternates between paratactic accumulation — the long list of towns joined by commas and 'and,' the catalogue of quantities — and hypotactic embedding through 'because,' 'that,' and 'which' clauses that qualify and subordinate. Neither mode dominates consistently.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Most sentences deliver their main predication early and trail qualifications afterward — 'But the mischief was this, that...,' 'It was therefore concluded, that...,' 'The good man Grangousier took great pleasure... and commanded...' The final exclamation is the only strongly periodic gesture.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is saturated with performable personality — mock-solemnity ('It was therefore concluded'), direct address, comic bathos, the narrator's interjection 'O the fair fecality.' Natural emphases, tonal shifts between gravity and grotesque, and the exclamatory finale all reward oral delivery.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The passage deliberately collides registers: Latinate ceremonial diction ('ingrediency,' 'fecality,' 'admonitions,' 'undecent') crashes against low Anglo-Saxon earthiness ('stunk,' 'gulched up,' 'shitten stuff,' 'ordure'). The comic effect depends entirely on this collision.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose constantly draws attention to its own surface through mock-heroic inflation, the absurd precision of the quantity catalogue ('sixteen quarters, two bushels, three pecks and a pipkin full'), the invented Latinate coinage 'ingrediency,' and the exclamatory rhetorical flourish at the close — the language performs itself as language.

text: Well, the priest did very well, considering. He got in all the details, and that is a good thing in a local item: you see, he had kept books for the undertaker-department of his church when he was younger, and there, you know, the money's in the details; the more details, the more swag: bearers, mutes, candles, prayers --everything counts; and if the bereaved don't buy prayers enough you mark up your candles with a forked pencil, and your bill shows up all right. And he had a good knack at getting in the complimentary thing here and there about a knight that was likely to advertise--no, I mean a knight that had influence; and he also had a neat gift of exaggeration, for in his time he had kept door for a pious hermit who lived in a sty and worked miracles.
source: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs drive the passage throughout — kept, got, counts, mark up, shows up, advertise, worked — with human agents performing concrete actions. Nominalizations are minimal and functional rather than structural.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage mixes both modes: paratactic chains run through the list ('bearers, mutes, candles, prayers') and coordinate clauses ('and he had a good knack... and he also had'), but hypotactic subordination appears in 'when he was younger,' 'if the bereaved don't buy,' and 'who lived in a sty.'
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive immediately and qualifications trail behind — 'He got in all the details, and that is a good thing' — with the prose accumulating observations in forward motion rather than suspending resolution.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is saturated with performable personality — the conspiratorial 'you see,' the self-correcting 'no, I mean,' the deadpan 'a pious hermit who lived in a sty.' There are natural emphases, comic pauses, and a distinct speaking presence throughout.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Predominantly Anglo-Saxon and colloquial diction: swag, knack, neat, mark up, shows up, sty. The register is deliberately vernacular and demotic, with Latinate words ('bereaved,' 'exaggeration') used for comic incongruity.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws constant attention to its own surface through the narrator's self-interruption ('no, I mean'), the comic list structure, the ironic juxtaposition of ecclesiastical and commercial vocabularies, and the deadpan understatement of the final clause — all foregrounding the writing as performance.

text: The ungentle laws and customs touched upon in this tale are historical, and the episodes which are used to illustrate them are also historical. It is not pretended that these laws and customs existed in England in the sixth century; no, it is only pretended that inasmuch as they existed in the English and other civilizations of far later times, it is safe to consider that it is no libel upon the sixth century to suppose them to have been in practice in that day also. One is quite justified in inferring that whatever one of these laws or customs was lacking in that remote time, its place was competently filled by a worse one. The question as to whether there is such a thing as divine right of kings is not settled in this book. It was found too difficult. That the executive head of a nation should be a person of lofty character and extraordinary ability, was manifest and indisputable; that none but the Deity could select that head unerringly, was also manifest and indisputable; that the Deity ought to make that selection, then, was likewise manifest and indisputable; consequently, that He does make it, as claimed, was an unavoidable deduction. I mean, until the author of this book encountered the Pompadour, and Lady Castlemaine, and some other executive heads of that kind; these were found so difficult to work into the scheme, that it was judged better to take the other tack in this book (which must be issued this fall), and then go into training and settle the question in another book. It is, of course, a thing which ought to be settled, and I am not going to have anything particular to do next winter anyway.
source: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose mixes nominal constructions ('divine right of kings,' 'unavoidable deduction,' 'lofty character and extraordinary ability') with active verbs and first-person agency ('I am not going to have,' 'it was judged,' 'encountered'). Neither mode dominates; the nominalizations tend to cluster in the mock-logical middle section while the framing sentences are more verb-driven.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage alternates between hypotactic embedding ('inasmuch as they existed,' 'that none but the Deity could select') and paratactic coordination, especially in the final sentences where clauses are strung together with 'and.' The mock-syllogism section is heavily hypotactic; the deflating conclusion collapses into parataxis.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The triadic 'that X was manifest and indisputable' construction is periodic, suspending resolution across three parallel subordinate clauses before delivering 'consequently.' But the surrounding sentences are running, delivering their main predications early and trailing qualifications — most notably the final sentence, which arrives at its punchline immediately and then adds the comic afterthought.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is deeply performable — the mock-solemn buildup of the syllogism invites a rising, portentous delivery that is then punctured by 'I mean, until the author of this book encountered the Pompadour.' The parenthetical '(which must be issued this fall)' and the final throwaway line demand comic timing and a specific ironic register.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The passage deliberately plays high register against low — formal Latinate diction ('manifest and indisputable,' 'unerringly,' 'unavoidable deduction') is undercut by colloquial deflation ('take the other tack,' 'go into training,' 'I am not going to have anything particular to do next winter anyway'). The comic effect depends entirely on this register collision.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose constantly draws attention to its own surface through structural display — the triadic parallel construction of the syllogism, the sudden shift to first person ('I mean'), the self-referential parenthetical about publication, and the bathetic final sentence. These are deliberate rhetorical figures that foreground the writing as performance rather than transparent argument.

text: As to my own treatment while I lived on Colonel Lloyd’s plantation, it was very similar to that of the other slave children. I was not old enough to work in the field, and there being little else than field work to do, I had a great deal of leisure time. The most I had to do was to drive up the cows at evening, keep the fowls out of the garden, keep the front yard clean, and run of errands for my old master’s daughter, Mrs. Lucretia Auld. The most of my leisure time I spent in helping Master Daniel Lloyd in finding his birds, after he had shot them. My connection with Master Daniel was of some advantage to me. He became quite attached to me, and was a sort of protector of me. He would not allow the older boys to impose upon me, and would divide his cakes with me.
source: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs carry the prose throughout — drive, keep, run, spent, shot, became, divide, impose, allow. Nominalizations are minimal and incidental ('connection,' 'advantage,' 'treatment'), never chained into prepositional phrase clusters.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage mixes both modes: the list of chores ('drive up the cows... keep the fowls... keep the front yard... run of errands') is paratactic, while subordinating constructions appear in 'after he had shot them' and 'He would not allow the older boys to impose upon me.' Neither dominates decisively.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive early and consistently — 'I was not old enough,' 'I had a great deal of leisure time,' 'He became quite attached to me' — with qualifications trailing afterward rather than suspending the main clause.
claude_justifications.voice: The first-person narration carries a distinct, performable cadence — plain, measured, and quietly dignified. The final two short sentences ('He would not allow... and would divide his cakes with me') have a natural rise and fall that rewards oral delivery.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Predominantly Anglo-Saxon diction: cows, fowls, yard, cakes, birds, boys, field, old. The few Latinate words ('leisure,' 'connection,' 'advantage,' 'protector') are common enough to feel unmarked rather than elevated.
claude_justifications.opacity: The language effaces itself entirely in service of the narrative content — no sound patterns, rhetorical figures, or structural display draw attention to the prose surface. The reader looks straight through to the described experience.

text: 25:18 And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the door: 25:19 And out of the city he took an officer that was set over the men of war, and five men of them that were in the king’s presence, which were found in the city, and the principal scribe of the host, which mustered the people of the land, and threescore men of the people of the land that were found in the city: 25:20 And Nebuzaradan captain of the guard took these, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah: 25:21 And the king of Babylon smote them, and slew them at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away out of their land.
source: King James Bible, King James Bible

claude_justifications.nounVerb: The prose moves through a chain of concrete actions — took, found, mustered, brought, smote, slew, was carried away — with human agents performing each. Nominal phrases name persons and roles but do not suppress action; the verbs carry the weight.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are coordinated almost entirely by 'and,' strung in an additive chain with no embedding through 'because,' 'although,' or 'since.' The relative clauses ('which were found,' 'which mustered') are appositional identifiers rather than true hypotactic subordination.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Each sentence delivers its main predication immediately — 'the captain took,' 'he took,' 'Nebuzaradan took,' 'the king smote' — with qualifications and enumerations trailing afterward in coordinate chains. Nothing is suspended or withheld.
claude_justifications.voice: The rhythmic accumulation of 'and... and... and' creates a performable cadence suited to oral recitation; the final sentence — 'So Judah was carried away out of their land' — lands with a weight that demands vocal emphasis and pause.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The diction is almost entirely Anglo-Saxon monosyllables — took, men, land, door, war, king, smote, slew — with no Latinate abstraction. The register is plain, concrete, and archaic-biblical rather than formal or elevated.
claude_justifications.opacity: The relentless polysyndetic 'and' pattern, the rhythmic enumeration of titles and persons, and the stark closing sentence ('So Judah was carried away out of their land') draw attention to the prose surface as a formal, liturgical structure — the style itself enacts the weight of the event.

text: {277} Now, I beheld in my dream, that they had not journeyed far, but the river and the way for a time parted; at which they were not a little sorry; yet they durst not go out of the way. Now the way from the river was rough, and their feet tender, by reason of their travels; so the souls of the pilgrims were much discouraged because of the way. [Num. 21:4] Wherefore, still as they went on, they wished for better way. Now, a little before them, there was on the left hand of the road a meadow, and a stile to go over into it; and that meadow is called By-path Meadow. Then said Christian to his fellow, If this meadow lieth along by our wayside, let us go over into it. Then he went to the stile to see, and behold, a path lay along by the way, on the other side of the fence. It is according to my wish, said Christian. Here is the easiest going; come, good Hopeful, and let us go over.
source: John Bunyan, Pilgrim's Progress

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs drive the narrative throughout — beheld, journeyed, parted, durst, wished, went, lay — with minimal nominalization. Even abstract states are rendered through verbal action: 'the souls of the pilgrims were much discouraged because of the way' keeps the predication in the verb rather than collapsing it into a noun phrase.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are chained by 'and,' 'but,' 'yet,' and 'now' in the additive biblical manner, with very little subordination. The connective tissue is coordinative throughout, giving the passage its characteristic accumulative rhythm.
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive immediately and early — 'they had not journeyed far,' 'the way from the river was rough,' 'a little before them, there was a meadow' — with qualifications trailing afterward. There is no suspension of the main clause behind introductory material.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is strongly performable: the repeated 'Now' functions as a storyteller's beat, the direct speech ('Here is the easiest going; come, good Hopeful') invites vocal characterization, and the rhythmic biblical cadences create natural rises and falls for oral delivery.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: Diction is overwhelmingly Anglo-Saxon and monosyllabic — way, road, feet, path, fence, stile, rough, tender — with the plain register of the King James Bible. The few Latinate words ('discouraged,' 'meadow') are fully domesticated into common usage.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose draws attention to its own surface through the ritualized repetition of 'Now' as a narrative marker, the allegorical naming convention ('By-path Meadow'), and the deliberate biblical cadence that signals genre and invites the reader to notice the form as form. The prose is not merely transparent reportage but a consciously styled imitation of scriptural narrative.

text: 12:17 Moreover the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 12:18 Son of man, eat thy bread with quaking, and drink thy water with trembling and with carefulness; 12:19 And say unto the people of the land, Thus saith the Lord GOD of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and of the land of Israel; They shall eat their bread with carefulness, and drink their water with astonishment, that her land may be desolate from all that is therein, because of the violence of all them that dwell therein. 12:21 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 12:22 Son of man, what is that proverb that ye have in the land of Israel, saying, The days are prolonged, and every vision faileth? 12:23 Tell them therefore, Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will make this proverb to cease, and they shall no more use it as a proverb in Israel; but say unto them, The days are at hand, and the effect of every vision.
source: King James Bible, King James Bible

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active imperatives and verbs drive the prophetic commands — eat, drink, say, tell, cease — but nominal phrases also carry significant weight: 'the violence of all them that dwell therein,' 'the effect of every vision.' Neither mode fully dominates.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: The passage is structured almost entirely through coordinate 'and' chains in the Hebrew-via-KJV manner — 'eat thy bread... and drink thy water... and say unto the people' — with only shallow subordination ('that her land may be desolate,' 'because of the violence').
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: Main predications arrive immediately and accumulate forward — 'eat thy bread with quaking, and drink thy water with trembling' — without suspended or front-loaded subordinate structures holding back the main clause.
claude_justifications.voice: The prose is built for oral delivery and performance: direct address ('Son of man'), repeated divine attribution ('Thus saith the Lord GOD'), imperative commands, and the rhythmic parallelism of 'eat... drink... eat... drink' all demand a performing voice with dynamic range.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The diction is overwhelmingly Anglo-Saxon and monosyllabic — bread, land, days, hand, word, eat, drink, cease — with only a few Latinate intrusions ('inhabitants,' 'astonishment,' 'prolonged') that sit as elevated exceptions in an otherwise plain register.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose foregrounds its own surface through deliberate structural repetition — the doubled 'eat/drink' parallelism, the formulaic 'Thus saith the Lord GOD,' the antithetical reversal of 'The days are prolonged' against 'The days are at hand' — all of which draw attention to the language as formal, ritualized display.

text: But my intention is very far from being confined to provide only for the children of professed beggars: it is of a much greater extent, and shall take in the whole number of infants at a certain age, who are born of parents in effect as little able to support them, as those who demand our charity in the streets. As to my own part, having turned my thoughts for many years upon this important subject, and maturely weighed the several schemes of our projectors, I have always found them grossly mistaken in their computation. It is true, a child just dropt from its dam, may be supported by her milk, for a solar year, with little other nourishment: at most not above the value of two shillings, which the mother may certainly get, or the value in scraps, by her lawful occupation of begging; and it is exactly at one year old that I propose to provide for them in such a manner, as, instead of being a charge upon their parents, or the parish, or wanting food and raiment for the rest of their lives, they shall, on the contrary, contribute to the feeding, and partly to the clothing of many thousands.
source: Jonathan Swift, A Modest Proposal

claude_justifications.nounVerb: Active verbs with a first-person agent appear throughout ('I propose,' 'I have always found,' 'having turned my thoughts'), but nominalizations and noun-heavy constructions also carry significant weight ('computation,' 'nourishment,' 'occupation,' 'intention'). Neither mode fully dominates.
claude_justifications.parataxisHypotaxis: Clauses are deeply embedded through 'who,' 'which,' 'as,' 'that,' and participial constructions, creating multiple levels of subordination — the final sentence alone suspends its resolution through a long chain of 'instead of... or... or...' before arriving at 'they shall, on the contrary, contribute.'
claude_justifications.periodicRunning: The passage repeatedly delays its main predications behind qualifying and conditional material — most strikingly in the final sentence, where the main clause ('they shall contribute') is held back through an elaborate series of negative conditions and participial phrases that must be traversed first.
claude_justifications.voice: The first-person projector's voice is insistently present and performable — the dry precision of 'a solar year,' the clinical 'dropt from its dam,' and the mock-modest 'as to my own part' all create natural emphases and a tone of ironic self-satisfaction that rewards oral delivery.
claude_justifications.primaryRegister: The prose deliberately mixes registers for satirical effect: formal Latinate diction ('computation,' 'nourishment,' 'raiment,' 'maturely weighed') sits alongside brutally plain Anglo-Saxon terms ('dam,' 'dropt,' 'scraps,' 'begging'), and the collision between the two is the central rhetorical device.
claude_justifications.opacity: The prose constantly draws attention to its own surface through the ironic gap between its bureaucratic precision ('exactly at one year old,' 'not above the value of two shillings') and its monstrous content — the language itself is the joke, and the reader cannot look through it to content without noticing the performance of reasonableness.
